An AI chip startup just doubled its valuation to US$21 billion in under a month. The interesting part isn't the number — it's what the money is betting on.

Etched raised US$700 million in a round led by trading firm Jane Street, which had tested the hardware and now runs one of Etched's racks in its own datacentre. Kleiner Perkins, Sequoia, Andreessen Horowitz and Tiger Global are among the other investors. The company was valued at around US$10.3 billion in July.

Three days at Hot Chips 2026, and the center of gravity wasn't a chip. It was a constraint.

Every headline architecture — Google splitting TPU into separate training and serving chips, Intel dropping HBM entirely on Crescent Island, OpenAI's Jalapeño, Qualcomm burying compute under LPDDR, SanDisk stacking NAND into HBM's form factor — was a different answer to the same question: not how fast you can compute, but where you can hold the weights and how far they have to travel.

Etched vs NVIDIA: What you need to know
The AI chip battle is getting interesting.

NVIDIA builds GPUs that can handle almost everything training, inference, different models, and workloads.

Etched is taking the opposite approach.

Its Sohu chip is built specifically for Transformer-based AI inference.
The bet is simple:
NVIDIA: Flexibility
Etched: Specialization

Etched claims its Sohu systems can deliver 500K+ tokens/sec on Llama 70B, dramatically above comparable GPU setups but these numbers are still largely company-reported.

And NVIDIA isn't sitting still either. Its latest inference-focused systems show that it's also optimizing heavily for agentic AI and token generation.

I've been waiting two years for this chip.

Back in June 2024, Etched came out of stealth with a pitch that sounded insane: build the chip specifically for transformer inference, not as a general-purpose GPU. One Etched server potentially replacing 160 NVIDIA H100s.

I chose to pay very close attention. Not because I knew they were right — nobody knew — but because the idea made sense.

GPUs won AI because they were already there: massively parallel, programmable, backed by NVIDIA's software ecosystem.
